title: Can You Own a Sugar Glider in Utah? What the Law Actually Says - NewsBreak
text:
By Animal of Things Editorial ,
10 hours ago Explore amazing animal stories – visit Animal of Things Now and follow us!
If you’ve been thinking about bringing a sugar glider home in Utah, the short answer is yes — state law generally allows it. But the longer answer involves local ordinances, the Utah Division of Wildlife Resources, and a few details that are easy to overlook until it’s too late.
Sugar gliders ( Petaurus breviceps ) are small, nocturnal marsupials native to Australia, Indonesia, and Papua New Guinea. They have become increasingly popular as pets due to their unique appearance and sociable nature. Before you commit to ownership, though, you need a clear picture of what Utah law requires — and what your city or county may prohibit on top of that.
Is It Legal to Own a Sugar Glider in Utah? Sugar gliders are legal to own as pets in most U.S. states, and Utah is included among those states where ownership is permitted. That said, legality at the state level does not automatically mean you can keep one anywhere in Utah without restriction.
Sugar gliders are not currently protected by any national laws or import restrictions, but exotic pet ownership is regulated at the state, county, or city level, so you need to check your specific jurisdiction. Utah is a good example of exactly why that matters — the state says yes, but at least one major city says no.
Pro Tip: Before purchasing a sugar glider, call your city hall or county animal control office directly to confirm local rules. Online sources may not reflect the most recent ordinance changes.
Continue exploring: Is It Legal to Own a Fox in Delaware? What You Need to Know
If you’re researching exotic pet laws in other states, it’s worth knowing that rules vary widely. For example, Colorado and Arizona each have their own frameworks that differ from Utah’s approach.
Utah’s Laws on Sugar Glider Ownership Utah’s exotic animal rules fall primarily under the Utah Division of Wildlife Resources (DWR) and the state’s administrative code. The rules concern the collection, importation, and possession of zoological animals, though commonly kept domestic animals such as cats, dogs, gerbils, and hamsters are not governed by these rules.
A person must obtain a certificate of registration before collecting, importing, transporting, or possessing any species of animal classified as prohibited or controlled. The key question for sugar glider owners is which classification applies. Under the previous version of the Utah Administrative Code (R657-3), sugar gliders were listed as “noncontrolled,” meaning animals in that category required no certification or registration — sugar gliders were classified as noncontrolled and were legal to have as pets without any state-level permit.
The original R657-3 rule was repealed in August 2023 and replaced by updated rules R657-3a and R657-3b. It is the responsibility of any person who obtains a certificate of registration to read, understand, and comply with the rule and all other applicable federal, state, county, city, or other municipality laws, regulations, and ordinances governing animals. Because the regulatory framework has been updated, confirming sugar gliders’ current classification directly with the DWR is the safest step you can take.
Under Utah state law, private citizens may not possess dangerous wild animals, such as large carnivores or certain venomous reptiles, without a required permit from the Division of Wildlife Resources. Sugar gliders do not fall into the dangerous wildlife category, which supports their general permissibility under state law.

Key Insight: Utah’s wildlife regulations were significantly updated in August 2023. If you read older articles stating sugar gliders are “completely unregulated” in Utah, those references may be based on the repealed R657-3 rule. Always verify with the DWR directly at wildlife.utah.gov .
Wondering how Utah compares to neighboring states? Washington and Texas both permit sugar gliders but operate under different regulatory structures worth reviewing if you move or travel with your pet.
Permits or Requirements to Own a Sugar Glider in Utah The permit picture in Utah is one of the more debated aspects of sugar glider ownership in the state. Sugar gliders are classified as exotic animals rather than domesticated pets in Utah, and state law requires individuals who wish to own one to obtain a permit. Some sources, however, point to the prior noncontrolled classification as evidence that no state permit is needed.
To legally own a sugar glider in Utah under the permit framework, you would apply for an Exotic Animal Permit from the Division of Wildlife Resources (DWR), a process that typically involves submitting necessary paperwork and paying an associated fee. Given the August 2023 regulatory update, it’s worth confirming whether the DWR now treats sugar gliders as noncontrolled (no permit needed) or controlled (permit required) under the new rule structure.
It is unlawful to possess an animal for which a certificate of registration is required if you do not have a valid certificate, and any live animals held under an expired certificate may be seized by the division. If a permit is ultimately required for your situation, keeping it current is just as important as obtaining it in the first place.
Related article: Can You Own a Wolf in South Carolina? What State Law Actually Says
Unpermitted animals may be seized immediately if you cannot produce a valid permit for each individual animal, and you may be given a citation for illegal possession, which is a Class B misdemeanor.
Requirement Details Governing agency Utah Division of Wildlife Resources (DWR) Permit type (if required) Certificate of Registration / Exotic Animal Permit Application process Paperwork submission and associated fee to the DWR Renewal Must be renewed before expiration to avoid unlawful possession Release to wild Prohibited without written DWR authorization Local Laws That May Apply in Utah This is where Utah gets complicated. Even if state law permits sugar gliders, your city or county may not. Even in states where sugar gliders are legal at the state level, local laws may impose additional restrictions on ownership, and Utah is a clear example — sugar gliders are illegal in Salt Lake City.
Because local ordinances can differ significantly, it is important to verify regulations at the city or county level before acquiring a sugar glider. Salt Lake City is the most well-documented example in Utah, but it is not the only municipality worth checking. Cities like Holladay have their own exotic animal permit requirements baked into local code. Under Holladay’s city code, it is unlawful for any person to own or keep an exotic animal without a permit.
Just because an animal is legal to own in the state does not mean the city you live in allows it, and many local cities and counties have their own restrictions on which animals are legal to keep — you should check with your local city and/or county for their specific regulations.
Salt Lake City: Sugar gliders are reported to be prohibited under local ordinance. Holladay: An exotic animal permit is required to own or keep any exotic animal. Other cities and counties: Rules vary — contact your local animal control office or city hall to confirm. It is your responsibility to comply with all local laws, ordinances, and covenants before importing or possessing live wildlife. This applies whether you’re in Provo, Ogden, St. George, or anywhere else in the state.

Other states with active local-level restrictions offer useful context. Minnesota has a similar situation where the state permits sugar gliders but St. Paul prohibits them, and New York bans them within New York City while allowing them elsewhere in the state.
Penalties for Illegally Owning a Sugar Glider in Utah Utah takes unpermitted exotic animal possession seriously. Unpermitted animals may be seized immediately by the DWR, Department of Health, the Department of Agriculture and Food, animal control officers, or peace officers if you cannot produce a valid permit for each individual animal.
You may be written a citation for illegally possessing these animals, which is a Class B misdemeanor. In Utah, a Class B misdemeanor can carry fines and potential jail time, making the cost of non-compliance far higher than the cost of doing the paperwork correctly upfront.
A person may not release from captivity any bird or mammal without first obtaining written authorization from the division, and any peace officer, division representative, or authorized animal control officer may seize, euthanize, or dispose of any live bird or mammal that is released from or escapes from captivity. This is an important point for sugar glider owners: if your glider escapes, you could face additional legal consequences beyond simple possession violations.
Important Note: Penalties can stack if you’re also in violation of a local ordinance on top of a state-level infraction. A citation from animal control and a state wildlife violation are separate matters that may be pursued independently.

Ignorance of the law is not a good defense, and if you acquire an illegal pet you may face confiscation of your pet and possibly even euthanasia of your pet down the road. The stakes are real, both financially and emotionally.
For comparison, states like Virginia and Ohio have their own penalty structures for illegal exotic pet possession that follow a similar pattern of seizure and misdemeanor charges.
What to Know Before Getting a Sugar Glider in Utah Assuming you’ve confirmed that sugar gliders are permitted in your specific city or county, there are several practical considerations that go beyond legal compliance. The care, diet, and housing needs of this species are extremely difficult to meet for its lifetime, and potential owners are unlikely to be able to provide a good quality of life without significant preparation.
Sugar gliders are often imported from Indonesia, and there is an increased conservation and zoonotic disease risk from animals originating from the wild — however, sugar gliders are also captive bred in the U.S., and animals sourced from captive breeding have a reduced risk of carrying zoonotic diseases. Choosing a reputable, USDA-licensed breeder is one of the most important decisions you’ll make.
In the wild, sugar gliders live in highly social groups, gliding tree to tree and communicating through scent and calls — in captivity, they should be housed with other sugar gliders and provided an environment that allows leaping and climbing, with enriching toys and nesting boxes. Keeping a single glider without social companionship is widely considered a welfare concern.

Verify legality with your city or county before purchasing. Contact the Utah Division of Wildlife Resources to confirm current permit requirements under the updated R657-3a/3b rules. Source your sugar glider from a captive-bred, USDA-licensed breeder. Plan for a pair — sugar gliders are social animals and do poorly in isolation. Find an exotic mammal veterinarian in your area before bringing your glider home. Never release a captive sugar glider into the wild. You should ensure you have access to a veterinarian specializing in exotic mammals and consult them about proper habitat setup, diet, and care. Most standard veterinary practices do not see exotic marsupials, so finding the right vet in advance — rather than in an emergency — is a step that saves stress and potentially your pet’s life.
It is crucial not to release captive-bred sugar gliders into the wild, as they may disrupt local ecosystems or struggle to survive without human assistance. Utah’s native ecosystem is not suited to support a non-native marsupial population, and releasing one is both an ecological concern and a legal violation.
If you want to learn more about the different varieties available before committing, exploring the different types of sugar gliders can help you understand what you’re getting into. And if you’re curious how Utah’s rules stack up against other states, see how Indiana , Tennessee , and Georgia handle sugar glider ownership for additional context.
The bottom line: sugar gliders are generally permitted in Utah at the state level, but local restrictions — especially in Salt Lake City — can override that. Confirm your city’s rules, check in with the DWR on current permit requirements, and go into ownership with a clear understanding of both the legal and practical commitments involved.
